item.title: 9/UX brings a classic Mac feel to 9front
item.description: Bringing a classic MacOS Finder to Linux is all very well, but there's no shortage of Linux desktops… however, bringing one to 9front is even more unexpected – and even more useful. 9/UX is a new project by Jeff " Progrium " Lindsay, who was one of the people behind Docker, Webhooks, and more. When you follow that link, and you should, pay close attention to what looks like a screenshot at the top. It is not an image. It's a real live executing instance of the OS, running inside your web browser, running on top of hyper9 . (That is worth reading too – it's an impressive project in its own right.) As its GitHub repository describes, 9/UX is a "Macintosh-inspired graphical environment for 9front." The README provides more detail: "9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop experience (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata." Lindsay introduced 9/UX earlier this month in a short X thread , saying he "made my own kind of A/UX but on Plan 9." In its creator's own words, "it's slop", but this is kind of interesting, original, creative bot-assisted coding that we enjoy looking at. At the end of last week, he returned to explain more : "9/UX isn’t just a pretty Mac-style UI on Plan 9. It's filesystem inspectable. Shell scriptable. Even the Mac resource file format can be used through the filesystem." Regular readers may have noticed that The Reg FOSS desk is fascinated by Plan 9 and its FOSS continuation 9front. We've written and presented at length about this remarkable OS, and tried to explain its FOSS continuation 9front several times . But even with the best will we can muster, its unique GUI is not an especially friendly or easy one. Its idiosyncratic UI was inspired by the late great Niklaus Wirth 's unbelievably tiny Oberon OS, which we have written about before . It's cryptic, and that's being generous. The research and development effort that led to Unix didn't stop when Unix 7th Edition escaped from the Bell Labs in 1981 and mutated into Unix System III. The industry enthusiastically adopted System III and later System V. A decade after 7th Edition Unix, Linux became a GPL version of something very like that traditional Unix, closely followed by the BSDs – and between them, they have very effectively distracted most of the FOSS world ever since. Even so, Research Unix lived on, saw 8th, 9th, and 10th editions, and then was replaced by Plan 9. In 1996, many of Plan 9's limitations were overcome by Inferno – whose revival as InferNode we covered this week. We always vaguely thought that if 9front were to receive an improved GUI that was slightly more compliant with later GUI design standards, it might be with a version of the Inferno UI …

We always vaguely thought that if 9front were to receive an improved GUI that was slightly more compliant with later GUI design standards, it might be with a version of the Inferno UI … But apparently not. A new, easier, and yet still simple, clean and attractive desktop for 9front is here, and it looks like classic MacOS from the era of Apple's 68030 Unix A/UX. We do not think the chances are high that the 9front community will adopt this with enthusiasm. Even so, there is an AI programming manual for agents , and we've seen some interesting looking LLM-assisted 9front apps of late. Several can be found in the agent9 distributio n , which includes LLM-assisted ports of C++ , Python , and Rust , plus a version of DOSbox , and even a package manager called pac9 .®

item.title: ‘I’m loving it at Brugge’: Freddie Potts on going from West Ham’s bench to Champions League
item.description: Midfielder is preparing to face Liverpool after leaving the club he loves and overcoming a tough start in Belgium In April Freddie Potts was absorbing the disappointment of being substituted at half-time during West Ham’s FA Cup quarter-final defeat by Leeds. The midfielder was out of favour under Nuno Espírito Santo and could not have imagined that he would be preparing to face Liverpool in the Champions League seven months later. It is the 23-year-old’s reward for taking the difficult decision to leave his boyhood club last summer. Potts noticed his minutes were drying up in pre-season, even though West Ham were not exactly stocked with talent after relegation, and he was ready for a new challenge when Club Brugge offered about £10m to sign him. Continue reading...

item.title: GTA VI’s jaw-dropping success: in figures
item.description: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

item.title: Watch November's full Beaver Moon live online today with supermoon livestream
item.description: null Editor's Note: The Virtual Telescope Project's Nov. 24 stream has been cancelled due to clouds over the Manciana observation site in Italy. Be sure to check back tomorrow for our roundup of the best photos of the November supermoon! November's full moon rises tonight (Nov. 24)! You can see live telescopic views of the "Beaver supermoon" courtesy of the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP). The free YouTube livestream begins at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) and will feature live views of the moon captured by a suite of robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. Today's stream features expert commentary from VTP founder Gianluca Masi, along with photos of previous full moons shining above historic landmarks in the heart of Rome. What makes the November full moon special? November's full moon is often called the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the industrious animals are hard at work building dams and preparing for the winter months, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . It is also set to be a spectacular supermoon , which reaches peak illumination while within 90% of perigee — the closest point to Earth in the moon's 27-day elliptical orbit. You might like: November full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Beaver Moon . Supermoons can be up to 13% larger and 30% brighter than the smallest full moon of the year, which occurred in May earlier this year as the natural satellite shone opposite the sun in Earth's sky while close to apogee, when it is farthest from our planet. Interested in capturing your own mesmerizing views of the full moon? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the lunar disk , along with our roundups of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography . Editor's Note: If you would like to share your photos of the Beaver Moon with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), along with your name, location and thoughts to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: Nigeria and Tanzania to Co-Host Inaugural WHAS in Abuja, Mobilising Continental Action for Better Women’s Health
item.description: The Governments of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the United Republic of Tanzania will jointly host the inaugural Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) 2026 on Tuesday, 1 December 2026, at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja, from 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM. Held under the theme “Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health,” WHAS 2026 will convene approximately 300 senior decision-makers, including Heads of State, First Ladies, Ministers of Health and Finance, African Union (AU) leadership, development finance institutions, philanthropists, and health innovators, to move Africa from political commitment to accountable investment and delivery. As a Nigeria-led, African-owned continental platform, WHAS is designed to advance women’s health across the entire life course, encompassing maternal, reproductive, and gynaecological health, noncommunicable diseases, and menopause, by treating women’s health not merely as a social priority, but as a central driver of Africa’s economic and social progress. Investing in women’s health is also an investment in Africa’s productivity, economic resilience, and future prosperity. item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.content:encoded: The Governments of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the United Republic of Tanzania will jointly host the inaugural Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) 2026 on Tuesday, 1 December 2026, at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja, from 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM. Held under the theme “Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health,” WHAS 2026 will convene approximately 300 senior decision-makers, including Heads of State, First Ladies, Ministers of Health and Finance, African Union (AU) leadership, development finance institutions, philanthropists, and health innovators, to move Africa from political commitment to accountable investment and delivery. As a Nigeria-led, African-owned continental platform, WHAS is designed to advance women’s health across the entire life course, encompassing maternal, reproductive, and gynaecological health, noncommunicable diseases, and menopause, by treating women’s health not merely as a social priority, but as a central driver of Africa’s economic and social progress. Investing in women’s health is also an investment in Africa’s productivity, economic resilience, and future prosperity. WHAS 2026 bridges the flagship African Union Champion mandates of the two co-hosting nations. Serving as founding convener, Nigeria brings the political leadership and health workforce agenda championed by His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, AU Champion for Human Resources for Health and Community Health Delivery Partnership. Nationally, WHAS is anchored in the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare under the leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, CON , with presidential facilitation by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Women’s Health (OSSAP-WH) . As co-host, Tanzania brings its continental leadership on maternal and child health, championed by Her Excellency, President Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, AU Champion for Maternal and Child Health, advancing the Continental Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) 2026–2030 and its Three Zeros: Zero Home Delivery, Zero Preventable Maternal and Newborn Deaths, and Zero Unvaccinated Children. Tanzania’s co-hosting is delivered through the Ministry of Health, led by Hon. Mohamed Omary Mchengerwa , Minister of Health, and the Secretariat of the African Union Champion for Maternal and Child Health. Speaking ahead of WHAS 2026, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, CON , Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, described the Summit as an important platform for advancing collaboration, shared learning, and African ownership of the women’s health agenda: “ The Women’s Health Africa Summit is a great platform for bringing together leaders, advocates, practitioners, academics and financiers to identify gaps, mobilise action and facilitate shared learning across countries. Indeed, women’s health is a global issue, and even wealthier countries continue to face significant gaps in this area. Ultimately, responsibility lies with us as leaders on the continent. We must take ownership of our health priorities.” Echoing the commitment to continental solidarity and measurable progress, Hon. Ummy Ally Mwalimu , Special Adviser to the President of the United Republic of Tanzania on Maternal and Child Health and Head of the Secretariat of the African Union Champion for Maternal and Child Health, highlighted the synergy between both nations’ leadership agendas: “Under the leadership of Her Excellency President Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, AU Champion for Maternal and Child Health, Tanzania is proud to co-host WHAS with Nigeria. Collaboration between our two AU Champions is an implementation imperative, not simply a matter of institutional goodwill. Coordinated leadership is essential to align workforce investment, community health delivery, sustainable financing and accountability with country-led priorities, avoid fragmented efforts and translate continental commitments into measurable results. The Three Zeros of the Continental RMNCAH Roadmap depend on competent, adequately supported frontline health workers, functional referral systems and effective community outreach. WHAS, under the theme ‘Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health’, provides a timely platform for these shared commitments.” Pathfinder International , serving as Lead Technical Partner, is supporting programme design, technical content, strategic partnerships, and efforts to connect political leadership, financing, and country-led implementation, including practical follow-up beyond the Summit. Highlighting the broader vision of WHAS, Dr. Adanna Steinacker , Senior Special Assistant to the President on Women’s Health, noted: “ For too long, women’s health has been treated as a secondary concern or viewed narrowly through a single stage of life. WHAS changes that paradigm, bringing African governments, capital, and innovators together to back women’s health across the entire life course as a core pillar of our continent’s social and economic future.” Structured around three enduring pillars: Innovation, Financing, and Delivery , WHAS 2026 will focus on strengthening the frontline and specialist health workforce required to deliver quality care to women and girls at every stage of life. WHAS will seek to secure an initial set of country and institutional commitments, including accelerated action on neglected gynaecological conditions, while establishing an enduring framework for African-led collaboration and post-summit accountability. Event : Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) 2026 Date : Tuesday, 1 December 2026 Time : 12:00 PM – 7:00 PM WAT Venue : State House Banquet Hall, Abuja, Nigeria Theme : Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health Co-Hosts : Federal Republic of Nigeria and United Republic of Tanzania Lead Technical Partner : Pathfinder International Related milestones : Joint Roadmap Dialogue, Addis Ababa, 24 November 2026; Political and Delivery Dialogue at WHAS, Abuja, 1 December 2026 For more information and partnerships, visit womenshealthafricasummit.com . About the Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) The Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) is a Nigeria-led, African-owned continental platform dedicated to advancing women’s health across the life course. Built on the three pillars of Innovation, Financing, and Delivery, WHAS brings together governments, political leaders, financing institutions, innovators, and delivery partners to strengthen health systems, mobilise domestic and international capital, and accelerate equitable access to quality healthcare for women across Africa. item.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
item.description: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system. “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said . Read full article Comments

item.title: CrowdStrike splashes $44B on Zscaler, customers brace for the bill
item.description: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals. The all-stock deal, announced on Monday , will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price. The transaction dwarfs even Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security upstart Wiz . Buying Zscaler gives CrowdStrike a sizeable foothold in the network security market, where it will be going up against the likes of Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet. The plan is to combine Falcon's endpoint protection capabilities with Zscaler's zero-trust network security technology, giving customers a single platform for securing devices and the connections between them. Naturally, there's an AI angle to the biggest cyber deal in history. CrowdStrike reckons owning both technologies will allow it to keep tabs on what AI agents are doing on corporate devices, where they're connecting, and what data they're getting their hands on. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz described the proposed combination as "cybersecurity’s operating system." The acquisition also gives CrowdStrike's salespeople plenty to get excited about. Around 8,000 Zscaler customers don't currently buy CrowdStrike's wares, and the companies already have more than 2,000 customers in common. CrowdStrike reckons it can boost its annualized revenue by around $1 billion within 30 months of closing the deal by selling more products to the two companies' existing customers. Some of those customers, however, don't sound particularly keen on being cross-sold to. Over on Reddit's r/sysadmin subreddit, news of the purchase was met with a familiar set of concerns from IT professionals who've lived through big-ticket enterprise software acquisitions before. "As a zscaler customer, this does worry me. Cost increase, forced move to Falcon, integration issues, etc," wrote one sysadmin. Another, whose organization already uses both vendors' products, added: "I think they're both great products but I imagine they'll jack up the price for our next renewal. Fun." CrowdStrike intends to make Zscaler's products available through its Falcon Flex licensing scheme, which allows customers to commit to a certain level of spending and pick and choose the products they deploy. Monday's acquisition announcement didn't spell out what the deal would mean for customers who want to continue using Zscaler alongside a rival endpoint security product. Others raised concerns about the fate of Red Canary, the managed detection and response specialist snapped up by Zscaler in August 2025. CrowdStrike already operates a competing service in Falcon Complete. There may also be some nervous employees at both companies. item.dc:creator: Carly Page
item.content:encoded: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals. The all-stock deal, announced on Monday , will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price. The transaction dwarfs even Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security upstart Wiz . Buying Zscaler gives CrowdStrike a sizeable foothold in the network security market, where it will be going up against the likes of Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet. The plan is to combine Falcon's endpoint protection capabilities with Zscaler's zero-trust network security technology, giving customers a single platform for securing devices and the connections between them. Naturally, there's an AI angle to the biggest cyber deal in history. CrowdStrike reckons owning both technologies will allow it to keep tabs on what AI agents are doing on corporate devices, where they're connecting, and what data they're getting their hands on. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz described the proposed combination as "cybersecurity’s operating system." The acquisition also gives CrowdStrike's salespeople plenty to get excited about. Around 8,000 Zscaler customers don't currently buy CrowdStrike's wares, and the companies already have more than 2,000 customers in common. CrowdStrike reckons it can boost its annualized revenue by around $1 billion within 30 months of closing the deal by selling more products to the two companies' existing customers. Some of those customers, however, don't sound particularly keen on being cross-sold to. Over on Reddit's r/sysadmin subreddit, news of the purchase was met with a familiar set of concerns from IT professionals who've lived through big-ticket enterprise software acquisitions before. "As a zscaler customer, this does worry me. Cost increase, forced move to Falcon, integration issues, etc," wrote one sysadmin. Another, whose organization already uses both vendors' products, added: "I think they're both great products but I imagine they'll jack up the price for our next renewal. Fun." CrowdStrike intends to make Zscaler's products available through its Falcon Flex licensing scheme, which allows customers to commit to a certain level of spending and pick and choose the products they deploy. Monday's acquisition announcement didn't spell out what the deal would mean for customers who want to continue using Zscaler alongside a rival endpoint security product. Others raised concerns about the fate of Red Canary, the managed detection and response specialist snapped up by Zscaler in August 2025. CrowdStrike already operates a competing service in Falcon Complete. There may also be some nervous employees at both companies. CrowdStrike is targeting $500 million in annual cost savings within two years of completing the acquisition, identifying datacenter infrastructure, supplier spending, and wider operations as areas where it can trim the fat. Neither company disclosed whether that would involve job cuts. Then there's the matter of putting more of the world's corporate security infrastructure in the hands of CrowdStrike, whose botched July 2024 software update took down an estimated 8.5 million Windows machines , grounding flights and disrupting hospitals, banks, and businesses worldwide. The incident gave IT departments a rather painful lesson in the risks of relying heavily on a single technology supplier. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, assuming regulators and Zscaler shareholders give it the green light. Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry will remain in charge of the business and take a seat on CrowdStrike's board. CrowdStrike reckons the combined business will have more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue when the deal closes. Judging by the reaction from some customers, they'll be keeping a particularly close eye on how much of that revenue comes from them. ®

item.title: One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job
item.description: My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don't meet your daily driving needs. It's tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you're holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren't hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use. The PhoneBox home screen displays useful stats and what's currently playing in your browser. Credit: Nick Indge I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in "the drawer." Launch applications on your PC from the connected Android device. Credit: Nick Indge Installation is a doddle Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn't have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you'd like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device. Read full article Comments

item.title: How Williams Alamu Graduated with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan
item.description: Williams Alamu marks his B.Sc. First-Class Honours graduation in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. There was a time when Williams Alamu would rather not sit an examination than risk getting a grade he wasn’t happy with. A B or a C in his Cambridge A-levels felt like a possibility he wasn’t ready to entertain, so he didn’t write the exams. A few years later, at 23, he has graduated from the University of Ibadan with a B.Sc. in Statistics, First-Class Honours and a CGPA of 3.65/4.0. Somewhere along the way, he decided that fear was no longer going to make his decisions for him. When Williams got into UI, he had a rather ambitious plan: become the Best Graduating Student in his faculty. Getting there would require more than good intentions. There were 5:30am wake-ups, difficult Statistics courses, friends who became unofficial tutors, a ChatGPT Pro subscription in 300 level, job offers he turned down and one Demography exam that kept him awake for 36 hours. University, as it turns out, came with quite a few plot twists. In this interview with BellaNaija, Williams takes us through the habits, people and decisions that shaped his academic journey. He also tells us whether he got that coveted top spot, what he learnt from the opportunities he put on hold, and what he would tell another student hoping to graduate with First-Class Honours. If that’s a goal you’re working towards, you may want to take notes. Literally or otherwise. Williams Alamu celebrates graduating with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. At what point did you realise you were chasing a record-breaking grade? Was it a goal from Day 1, or did it evolve? It was a goal from day one, actually. When I gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I already had my mind set on graduating as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty. I knew becoming the overall Best Graduating Student in the university would require an extraordinary amount of work, but I felt being the best in my faculty was something I wanted to work towards. And, of course, that would also mean graduating as the best student in my department. The motivation behind that goal goes back to shortly after secondary school, when my parents enrolled me in a Cambridge A-level programme. I went into it hoping to achieve three A-stars, but Chemistry was a major struggle. As the examinations approached, I became increasingly worried about my performance. I think I was more afraid of not meeting my own expectations than I was of the examination itself. The thought of getting a B or C frightened me so much that I eventually decided not to sit for the examinations. item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.content:encoded: Williams Alamu marks his B.Sc. First-Class Honours graduation in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. There was a time when Williams Alamu would rather not sit an examination than risk getting a grade he wasn’t happy with. A B or a C in his Cambridge A-levels felt like a possibility he wasn’t ready to entertain, so he didn’t write the exams. A few years later, at 23, he has graduated from the University of Ibadan with a B.Sc. in Statistics, First-Class Honours and a CGPA of 3.65/4.0. Somewhere along the way, he decided that fear was no longer going to make his decisions for him. When Williams got into UI, he had a rather ambitious plan: become the Best Graduating Student in his faculty. Getting there would require more than good intentions. There were 5:30am wake-ups, difficult Statistics courses, friends who became unofficial tutors, a ChatGPT Pro subscription in 300 level, job offers he turned down and one Demography exam that kept him awake for 36 hours. University, as it turns out, came with quite a few plot twists. In this interview with BellaNaija, Williams takes us through the habits, people and decisions that shaped his academic journey. He also tells us whether he got that coveted top spot, what he learnt from the opportunities he put on hold, and what he would tell another student hoping to graduate with First-Class Honours. If that’s a goal you’re working towards, you may want to take notes. Literally or otherwise. Williams Alamu celebrates graduating with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. At what point did you realise you were chasing a record-breaking grade? Was it a goal from Day 1, or did it evolve? It was a goal from day one, actually. When I gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I already had my mind set on graduating as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty. I knew becoming the overall Best Graduating Student in the university would require an extraordinary amount of work, but I felt being the best in my faculty was something I wanted to work towards. And, of course, that would also mean graduating as the best student in my department. The motivation behind that goal goes back to shortly after secondary school, when my parents enrolled me in a Cambridge A-level programme. I went into it hoping to achieve three A-stars, but Chemistry was a major struggle. As the examinations approached, I became increasingly worried about my performance. I think I was more afraid of not meeting my own expectations than I was of the examination itself. The thought of getting a B or C frightened me so much that I eventually decided not to sit for the examinations. Williams Alamu seated in a University of Ibadan lecture hall before a test during his Statistics degree. When I eventually gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I didn’t want to repeat that experience. I saw university as an opportunity to approach things differently. Rather than allow the fear of falling short to determine what I attempted, I wanted to embrace the challenge and give it my best effort. That’s where the ambition to become the Best Graduating Student in my faculty came from. In the end, I didn’t graduate as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty or department, but I graduated with a First Class, and that’s something I’m genuinely happy about. It wasn’t exactly the outcome I had envisioned, but unlike my experience with Cambridge A-levels, I didn’t allow the fear of falling short to stop me from trying. I set a goal, gave it my best effort, and saw it through. For me, that alone was a significant part of my growth. Explain your systems. Beyond “reading hard,” what were the specific study techniques or daily schedules that kept you at the top? I think one of the most important things I did was try my best not to miss classes. I attended a public university, so there were always distractions, but I made a conscious effort to be present. I wouldn’t say I paid 100% attention in every class, but I realised there was value in simply being there. Sometimes, lecturers made important statements or gave hints that proved useful in examinations. I also started studying by the fourth week of each semester, after giving myself some time to settle in and enjoy school. I would go over what had been taught that week and revisit earlier topics whenever I needed more background knowledge. Whenever I struggled with a question or finally understood a difficult concept, I took notes so I could return to them during examinations rather than start figuring things out all over again. Handwritten probability and mathematical Statistics notes from Williams Alamu’s study sessions at the University of Ibadan. I also relied heavily on my friends and was never ashamed to ask questions when I didn’t understand something. I was fortunate to have classmates who were willing to help, including Lateef Basunu , Akinmusire Esther , Moyosoluwa Opesitian , Shukuroh Oladokun , Franklin David and Samuel Okoosi . Lateef, in particular, was incredibly patient and would spend as much time as necessary explaining difficult concepts to me. I also learnt that I assimilated information better in the morning. I’ve always been an early riser, usually awake by 5:30 a.m., so I preferred to sleep early rather than force myself to study through the night. I made an effort to plan my days around my priorities. Looking back, there wasn’t one extraordinary technique behind my academic performance. It was a combination of attending classes, studying early, taking notes, asking questions and understanding when I worked best. Williams Alamu combines virtual study sessions with printed Statistics notes during his undergraduate studies at the University of Ibadan. What did you have to sacrifice? Tell us about the social events, personal time, hobbies or even sleep you had to put aside to protect your CGPA. I think the biggest sacrifices I made were actually in my career. Outside academics, I’m a designer, working primarily in product design and web experiences. As I grew in the field, more opportunities started coming my way, including full-time and remote job offers. However, combining those responsibilities with my academic workload was difficult, especially because I had already set a goal for myself at university. I remember receiving an offer to join a company as its founding designer just as I was about to begin my final examinations. There was also another opportunity involving relocation abroad. Both were opportunities I genuinely wanted, but I had invested so much in my education that I didn’t want to compromise on the academic goal I had set for myself. I wouldn’t say I sacrificed much socially, as I’ve never been someone who attends a lot of parties. My hobbies were a different story. I enjoy video games, but I deliberately waited until after university to buy the Nintendo Switch I had always wanted because I knew it could become another distraction. Sleep was another thing I occasionally sacrificed during examinations. I remember staying awake for almost 36 hours while preparing for a Demography examination, and there were other nights when I studied until 2 or 3 a.m. Looking back, university was about deciding what deserved my attention at different points. I couldn’t give everything the same level of attention, and for those four years, my academics had to take priority. Williams Alamu takes a break during an overnight study session in his department at the University of Ibadan. How did you handle the toughest courses or departmental hurdles that usually break a student’s GPA? I’ve always believed that when you don’t understand something, there’s no point pretending otherwise. Whenever I struggled with a course or topic, I sought help from people who understood it better. item.title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic
item.description: Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland. The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press . Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury , and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara . Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli. Read full article Comments

item.title: 18 brilliant and surprising gifts for science lovers this Christmas
item.description: This moon lamp is a hot Christmas tip from designer Phoebe Watts (see below) Gingko Design The New Scientist Christmas gift guide is assembled by our crack team of science editors and experts. If you’re struggling for gift ideas, you will find unexpected and ingenious suggestions for amateur astronomers and animal and nature lovers, as well as those fond of food, beauty and puzzles. And surely that covers all of us? Space reporter Leah Crane recommends the science-themed jigsaws from Nervous System Nervous System Puzzlingly beautiful: a science jigsaw If you’re looking for a quick and easy jigsaw to breeze through while watching holiday movies, Nervous System puzzles probably aren’t for you. But if you want something that’s part puzzle, part work of art, and that will keep you transfixed for hours, they’ll definitely do the trick. Nervous System makes laser-cut wooden puzzles with uniquely shaped pieces and science themes, and they are absolutely beautiful. I’m particularly a fan of their geode puzzles, featuring concentric wiggles of bright colour, including wiggly sides that defy every puzzler’s instinct to start with the edge pieces. For even more of a challenge, they make infinity puzzles that can be assembled and reassembled many different ways – those have no edge pieces at all, and some don’t even have a picture on them! Nervous System also sells absolutely stunning jewellery, lamps and sculptures, but to me the puzzles are the real show-stoppers. Nervous System puzzles , from $45 (£32) Advertisement Leah Crane The CL Companion 8×30 binoculars, as recommended by senior editor Chelsea Whyte Swarovski Optik Zoom in: splashing out on binoculars The eccentric filmmaker Werner Herzog famously declared that he travels with only a second set of underwear, a map, a toothbrush and a set of binoculars. I don’t travel quite so lightly, but on my next trip, I definitely want to add a pair of nice binos to my baggage. I tested out three sets at varying price levels, taking them down to my favourite spot on my local river and out to my backyard during a clear night with a half-moon overhead. The Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42 binoculars are extremely well balanced and were the most comfortable in my hands. They were particularly well-suited for twilight and brighter. The other Nikon set I tried was the Stabilised 12×25 S, which is much more compact. For my small hands that was fine, and the stabilisation was marvellous at reducing any shaking, both while looking at something fixed like the moon or moving quickly to track an eagle fishing for dinner. The stabilisation requires batteries, so these are probably best – suited to the more prepared adventurer. The stand – out pair was the CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik. I’ve never seen anything look better than they did through these lenses. They let in an enormous amount of light, making the world look like the brightness has been turned up. And the moon’s craters looked stunningly crisp. For the birdwatcher
item.dc:creator: New Scientist
item.content:encoded: This moon lamp is a hot Christmas tip from designer Phoebe Watts (see below) Gingko Design The New Scientist Christmas gift guide is assembled by our crack team of science editors and experts. If you’re struggling for gift ideas, you will find unexpected and ingenious suggestions for amateur astronomers and animal and nature lovers, as well as those fond of food, beauty and puzzles. I’m particularly a fan of their geode puzzles, featuring concentric wiggles of bright colour, including wiggly sides that defy every puzzler’s instinct to start with the edge pieces. Nervous System also sells absolutely stunning jewellery, lamps and sculptures, but to me the puzzles are the real show-stoppers. Nervous System puzzles , from $45 (£32) Advertisement Leah Crane The CL Companion 8×30 binoculars, as recommended by senior editor Chelsea Whyte Swarovski Optik Zoom in: splashing out on binoculars The eccentric filmmaker Werner Herzog famously declared that he travels with only a second set of underwear, a map, a toothbrush and a set of binoculars. I don’t travel quite so lightly, but on my next trip, I definitely want to add a pair of nice binos to my baggage. I tested out three sets at varying price levels, taking them down to my favourite spot on my local river and out to my backyard during a clear night with a half-moon overhead. The Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42 binoculars are extremely well balanced and were the most comfortable in my hands. They were particularly well-suited for twilight and brighter. The other Nikon set I tried was the Stabilised 12×25 S, which is much more compact. For my small hands that was fine, and the stabilisation was marvellous at reducing any shaking, both while looking at something fixed like the moon or moving quickly to track an eagle fishing for dinner. The stabilisation requires batteries, so these are probably best – suited to the more prepared adventurer. The stand – out pair was the CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik. I’ve never seen anything look better than they did through these lenses. They let in an enormous amount of light, making the world look like the brightness has been turned up. And the moon’s craters looked stunningly crisp. For the birdwatcher, wildlife lover or stargazer in your life, these would be a worthwhile, although pretty major, splurge. Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42 , £159 Nikon Stabilised 12×25 S , £729 CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik , from £1070 Chelsea Whyte Podcast editor Rowan Hooper’s tip this Christmas: the Magenta 5 bat detector Widcare Sounds good: a bat detector Thomas Nagel’s famous 1974 essay, “What is it like to be a bat?”, argued that we can never fully know the experience of being a bat (or any other animal). I have been testing that argument with my fantastic bat detector. The device picks up on the ultrasound frequencies emitted by bats as they fly overhead and converts them into clicks that we can hear. It also displays the frequency of the squeak, and that allows us to identify the species. In my London back garden I get mostly pipistrelles, our smallest bat at just 4 grams. Nagel is right – I don’t know what it is like to fly and catch moths by echolocation. But it is quite thrilling to hear the clicks as a bat swoops past in the dark, and that experience has got me a little closer to appreciating what it is like to be a bat. There are several options available, but I used the Magenta 5 bat detector from Wildcare. Magenta 5 bat detector , £105 Rowan Hooper Editor Catherine de Lange recommends the Timeshifter app Natee Meepian/Timeshifter Time for bed: a jet lag app If you have a jetsetter in your life, they are probably by definition the kind of person who is tricky to find a gift for. So why not gift them something money can’t buy (well, almost): an end to jet lag? Many moons ago, I was on a journalism fellowship about sleep at Harvard Medical School, when I visited the lab of sleep scientist Steven Lockley. I was fascinated by his experiments, including work he was doing with NASA astronauts, which looked at circadian rhythms, sleep and what happens when our bodies are out of sync with the natural rhythms of the day. Aside from astronauts, many of us who remain earthbound can still feel these effects – especially those who do regular shift work or long-distance travel. What’s more, a body clock that’s out of whack can have serious health consequences. I followed Lockley’s research closely over the years, and he was generous enough, whenever I travelled back to Boston, to make me a tailored jet-lag plan – when to sleep or nap in the days before and during my flight, as well as when to wear sunglasses and drink caffeine, all based on what time my flight was and the time difference. Fast forward about a decade, and this service is no longer a personal one – Lockley has created an app called Timeshifter, which allows users to plug in their flight details and instantly receive a step-by-step plan to minimise jet lag. There’s a version of the app for shift workers, too. I recently tried it on a trip to New York, purchasing a one-off plan rather than the subscription, and I can honestly say that I barely felt any jet lag at all – while my husband was falling asleep in his sushi at dinner. Timeshifter app , $6.99/month or $69.99/year (£5.30/month or £53/year) Catherine de Lange Environment reporter Madeleine Cuff recommends the Motus Strength II trainers Vivobarefoot Strong feet: barefoot trainers Forget spin classes and aerobics – fitness these days is all about strength over heart rate. If a loved one has started talking about “Lifting PBs” and “protein-maxxing”, you could do much worse than getting them some proper footwear for their gym trips. There’s emerging evidence to suggest barefoot trainers strengthen foot muscles compared with regular trainers, including the small, stabilising muscles that improve balance. Vivobarefoot’s Motus Strength are specifically designed for weightlifting sessions – I’ve been wearing them to the gym for the last few weeks and am a total convert. You can also get barefoot shoes for hiking and trail running, for those who prefer the great outdoors to the weights floor. Vivobarefoot Motus Strength , £150 Madeleine Cuff Video editor Emily Bates is enjoying these animal trading cards Life TGC Collect them all: animal trading cards If, like me, you grew up collecting Pokémon cards but now shudder at the prices and scalpers, there’s a brilliant alternative, and it’s science-themed. Life TCG lets players collect, trade and play using cards based on real-world creatures, with gameplay reminiscent of Top Trumps. But the artwork is the real highlight, a charming mix of realistic paintings, quirky cartoons and special-edition photography. One of my first packs even revealed a stunning South Chinese tiger card (one of my favourite animals). The gameplay itself is fairly simple, but the cards are beautiful enough to work as collectible art pieces in their own right. Better still, first-edition holographic cards are genuinely rare. Each is printed in numbers matching that animal’s estimated population in the wild. Life TCG also donates a portion of its profits to WWF.

item.title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
item.description: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday , Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday , almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday'

Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday , almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

item.title: My Experience at the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos
item.description: The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. When I got the email that I was selected for the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos, I knew, without doubt, that the cohort of writers I would engage with would be some of the finest around. I was not disappointed. The workshop put me in the same room with extremely talented writers I had read and admired from a distance. Some of us have shared publication credits and honours on longlists and shortlists of literary prizes over the past couple of years. For two days, we were guests of the British Council and students at the feet of our primary facilitator, Nigerian writer, journalist, and editor, Molara Wood . Liberian-American writer Wayétu Moore also facilitated a session, and a publishing masterclass was held by Anwuli Ojogwu and Eghosa Imasuen of Narrative Landscape Press. The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amodi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things. “Gotta Whack That Guy!” I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. These writers seemed assured in their craft, and it became further obvious as the conversations became robust. Molara Wood, with all her brilliance, struck me even more with the animated manner in which she facilitated the workshop. As though she was more excited to teach than we were to be taught by her. This made the workshop flow seamlessly from the jump. We shared opinions on the assigned short stories. We discussed how well they used dialogue, descriptions, and language to reveal so much about the characters and the world they inhabit. We discussed how words, accents, and other idiosyncrasies of characters can reveal class, age and societal standing. This is why it is important for writers to observe the world. To observe the minute details of what makes up people, because these are the tools through which subtext can be created. The arts are connected, especially through the basic principles of storytelling. Molara Wood recognised this by using the context of films, mostly classics, to highlight storytelling techniques for better understanding. The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amodi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things. “Gotta Whack That Guy!” I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. These writers seemed assured in their craft, and it became further obvious as the conversations became robust. Molara Wood, with all her brilliance, struck me even more with the animated manner in which she facilitated the workshop. As though she was more excited to teach than we were to be taught by her. This made the workshop flow seamlessly from the jump. We shared opinions on the assigned short stories. We discussed how well they used dialogue, descriptions, and language to reveal so much about the characters and the world they inhabit. We discussed how words, accents, and other idiosyncrasies of characters can reveal class, age and societal standing. This is why it is important for writers to observe the world. To observe the minute details of what makes up people, because these are the tools through which subtext can be created. The arts are connected, especially through the basic principles of storytelling. Molara Wood recognised this by using the context of films, mostly classics, to highlight storytelling techniques for better understanding. We discussed the dangers of anachronism in contemporary fiction through the critique of a Nigerian novel and the anachronistic elements therein. She hammered on the importance of reading widely, beyond the mainstream, beyond the contemporary, across literary cultures and traditions. We must read widely so we can know exactly what we are writing in response to. The workshop’s goal is in its name. The rudiments of writing are well known to writers, but not so much those of editing. To polish a story to the best it can be. “ To develop the inner practice of being attentive to define and understand the times ” . Editing one’s own work can be difficult. The sentimental value we place on our words makes it hard to, as they say, “kill your darlings”, but it is a necessity for the beauty of a story to shine through. For the writing to be better, we simply “Gotta whack that guy!” as Molara Wood called out from her workshop material. The afternoon session was facilitated by the Liberian-American novelist, Wayétu Moore. Her session was on Speculative fiction/Magical Realism. Naturally, the question raised is the extent to which these categorisations apply to the works of those who write from cultures where the material and the mystical spheres are considered to be in constant interaction. Such that the happenings that seem magical to a Western mind are random stories one hears from neighbours, friends and family so often that they are as real as anything, and an immutable fact. Tales of cats that bring down house walls, of children who die and return again and again, of grandfathers who come back as babies, of birds dropping from the sky and transforming into old women. Wayétu Moore was in conversation with us about this. The most important eye-opener for me during this session was about plot and character building. The rules for writing nuanced characters are the same regardless of whether a story is speculative or realist. Writers tend to venerate certain characters as saints and demonise others with no redeemable qualities, such that they are a clear antithesis of the other. But human beings are not that way. A supposedly evil character can be a loving husband. A torturer can be a caring father when he returns home every night. This is the nature of humans, the nature of the characters we want to portray in stories. It has been said that reality doesn’t necessarily make sense, but fiction should. The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. “Forget technique… Write from here.” We all had one question on our tongues on the second day of the workshop: who wrote the assigned anonymised short story we were to discuss? It was a shocking story, quality-wise, and was written by one of the greats of 20th-century African Writing, we came to find out. A story that meanders and pulls up new surprises with every line. In a workshop with a focus on editing, it was the perfect case study for our facilitator to have us note not only its obvious flaws, but also its strengths. We learned even more about dialogue and voice, structural and contextual editing. The field was covered. Molara Wood wanted to get as much as possible done despite the short time we had together for the workshop. So we had to eat into our lunch breaks, quite literally. No complaints; there was so much to converse about. The sessions were interactive. We discussed each other’s writing samples, and then our works-in-progress in pairs, giving feedback on what we thought worked well, what didn’t. A way of putting into practice what we had spent hours learning during the workshop. One that was soon reaching its end. When Eghosa Imasuen and Anwuli Ojogwu of Narrative Landscape Press filled the room with their presence for the afternoon session, I knew it was going to be enjoyable. Eghosa Imasuen is a very jovial man, mixing English with Pidgin to land a point and make jokes. It felt as if he knew us all beforehand. The publishing industry in Nigeria has always fascinated me. What are contracts like? How well do books sell? These things are often shrouded in mystery. Eghosa spearheaded the session. Anwuli made her points where she thought necessary. Understanding the publishing process within a Nigerian publishing house like NLP was necessary for writers who, after fine-tuning stories or a novel, would seek out publishers. The session included tips on how to put together a publisher’s query for a manuscript, and the fine margins that can make a query sound professional and confident. “Be simple. Less is more,” Anwuli noted. You write a good story, rewrite, revise, edit, put together a pack of publishers’ queries and send it off with a hail of prayers. “Writers are the suppliers of stories,” Eghosa Imasuen explained. Publishers produce and sell them. It is looking at stories in the business sense, because publishing is a business, a precarious, courageous one. This was further highlighted when we got into the numbers of it all, information that I was glad to be privy to. The nature of p

item.title: The Beatz Awards 2026: Soso Soberekon Honoured with Special Recognition Award as May D and Shiiro Light Up 11th Edition
item.description: The 11th edition of The Beatz Awards, held on Saturday, November 21, 2026, at the Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, Onikan, Lagos, was a remarkable celebration of music, creativity, excellence and the exceptional talents working behind the scenes of the Nigerian music industry. Under the theme “Behind the Beat, Beyond the Beat,” this year’s ceremony brought together music professionals, industry stakeholders, producers, songwriters, DJs, engineers, media personalities and other key players to celebrate the creative minds whose contributions continue to shape the sound and business of African music. Soso Soberekon Receives Special Recognition Award One of the major highlights of the evening was the presentation of the Special Recognition Award to renowned music executive and industry figure, Soso Soberekon, in recognition of his remarkable contributions to the Nigerian music industry. From talent discovery and artist development to music promotion, business development and industry connections, Soso Soberekon’s influence and commitment to the growth of Nigerian entertainment continue to resonate across different sectors of the culture. The special recognition celebrates his role in creating opportunities, supporting talents and contributing to the development of the Nigerian music ecosystem. May D and Shiiro Deliver Electrifying Performances The ceremony also featured captivating musical performances, with award-winning singer May D delivering an electrifying performance that got the audience on their feet, while producer and songwriter Shiiro equally thrilled guests with an impressive performance, showcasing the creativity and musical excellence that The Beatz Awards continues to celebrate. Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge: Kevwe Praise Emerges Winner Another major highlight of the 11th edition was the highly anticipated Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge, an initiative designed to discover, nurture and provide opportunities for emerging music producers. The competition provided a platform for talented producers who participated in the Beatz to Banger 2.0 training programme to showcase their creativity, technical abilities and music production skills before an audience of industry professionals. Following an intense competition among the final five contestants, Kevwe Praise emerged as the ultimate winner, earning the coveted title and a cash prize of ₦1.5 million. The winner’s cash cheque was presented by Princess Damilola Sonayon-James , APC Deputy Governorship Aspirant, alongside the Chief Executive Officer of The Beatz Awards, Elijah John . The moment marked a significant milestone for the winning producer and reinforced The Beatz Awards’ commitment to creating tangible opportunities for emerging talents beyond recognition and celebration. item.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
item.description: Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected. “It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. Advertisement In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective , it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage. Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter In the clinical trial , 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks. Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial. “These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney , the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end. “It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross. Read more You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think The medication also appeared safe. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected. “It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. Advertisement In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective , it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage. Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter In the clinical trial , 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks. Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial. “These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney , the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end. “It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross. Read more You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side-effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said. People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross. Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a trial of KT-621 in people with asthma , since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

item.title: BepiColombo takes the long way around Mercury after software glitch
item.description: A software fault cut short BepiColombo's Mercury orbit insertion burn, but the European Space Agency (ESA) says the mission remains on track to separate its two science orbiters on December 9. ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), still carrying JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), fired its four axial thrusters on November 21 to place the spacecraft in orbit. The burn began at 1824 UTC, when BepiColombo was approximately 635 km above the planet's surface. It was supposed to last for 37 minutes but shut down early . The shutdown , caused by a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, left the spacecraft in safe mode, a protective state in which all non-essential activities cease. Ignacio Tanco, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Operations Director, said: "Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened." The burn achieved around 77 percent of the planned velocity change, securing an orbit around Mercury but leaving BepiColombo taking 75 hours to circle the planet instead of the intended 58. The good news is that multiple burns were always going to be needed to adjust the orbit ahead of Mio separation and MPO reaching its science orbit. "The remaining MOI [Mercury Orbit Insertion] sequence has already been adapted to the new trajectory, with no additional burns required," ESA said. "After each burn, the Flight Dynamics team determines the achieved orbit to then design the next manoeuvre," said Frank Budnik, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Dynamics Manager. "So, the sequence is not only more propellant-efficient, it also allows Flight Dynamics to adapt each subsequent burn to the spacecraft's actual trajectory. It's a dynamic sequence! Each new manoeuvre is based on the previous ones." Teams at ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) and Airbus continue to investigate the underlying software fault. ESA has not said whether the revised burn sequence will affect propellant reserves available for a possible mission extension. The separation of Mio and MPO is planned for December 9, and more burns will be needed to guide MPO to its final orbit by March 2027, with science operations starting in April 2027. ®

item.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
item.description: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

item.title: November's full moon rises tonight! Here's how to see the Beaver Moon supermoon
item.description: null Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know. November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter. Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon , because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee , when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon". When to see the Beaver Moon November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon. A supermoon can make for a spectacular sight when caught close to the horizon. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. What should I expect from the November supermoon? You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering. Celestron Nexstar 4SE (Image credit: Celestron) This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. Check out our full Celestron Nexstar 4SE review for more. The supermoon will also appear particularly large while close to the horizon, as a phenomenon called the " moon illusion " tricks our brains into thinking that the lunar disk is larger while in the presence of foreground objects compared to when it is overhead.
