item.title: PSG had the best attack in Europe but Doué and Kvaratskhelia injuries will test Luis Enrique
item.description: Désiré Doué sustained an ACL injury in PSG’s 3-2 win at Nice and joins Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the treatment table By Get French Football News Luis Enrique is in uncharted territory, even if he insists that “it isn’t a first”. Since arriving at Paris Saint-Germain in 2023, only three players have spent more than 100 days on the sideline – Nuno Mendes, Lucas Hernandez and Presnel Kimpembe – and only Mendes is an important first-team player. But for the remainder of the season, or at least the vast majority of it, Luis Enrique must do without two of his stars: Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. Doué arrived in Nice on Saturday evening already bearing scars. The PSG forward wore a mouth guard after Davide Frattesi had dislodged one of his front teeth with a stray arm during France’s defeat by Italy during the international break. Continue reading...

item.title: Everything going down at once wasn't evidence of a conspiracy – but the truth may be scarier
item.description: Have you or someone you love been affected by a tech outage this week? Yeah, us too. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live In a week of big stories the biggest one seems to be the fact that everyone from Microsoft to the NSA was dealing with outages , and here's what might be the worst part: It doesn't seem to be AI, nor hostile countries intent on destroying our infrastructure. Unfortunately for all of us, what the past week of outages reveal is that – as we discussed on The Kettle less than a month ago – all of our essential tech infrastructure is basically held together with duct tape and twine. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo , cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons , and open source reporter Liam Proven to discuss what comes next, and whether we can fix any of this without tearing all of it out and starting from scratch. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:04) Hi everyone and welcome to the latest episode of the Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and if you're hearing this, then that means there isn't an outage right now, which seems like that might be a lot to ask of our technology in the past week. It's been a busy week. We had Anthropic's IPO , Nvidia drama continuing , and other stuff going on. But the one thing that everyone seems to be talking about is what's become known in the zeitgeist as Outagepalooza, as it seems like everything was offline at some point in the past few days. With me to discuss the chaos and the conspiracy theories they're giving rise to is Reg cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons and our open source reporter Liam Proven. Guys, what's happening? Jessica Lyons (00:45) I've got my tinfoil hat on right now, so I'm ready. Brandon (00:48) Yes, I've had family calling me being like, my god, what's happening? Who's ending the world right now? Is it AI? Jessica Lyons (00:55) Ha ha ha. Brandon (00:56) We'll get to that part. Liam Proven (00:57) Wonderful. My mum's wardrobe door stuck this week and we found a company on the little rock in the middle of the Irish Sea that fixes sliding doors and he didn't get my emails because he's one hundred percent Microsoft and he uses Hotmail and it's Hotmail. Liam Proven (01:18) And when I got it through, you'd be amazed at the ramifications. I SMS'd him in the end and he got that and then was really angry because I said, "Dude, I've been trying to get you for three days. Can you at least reply and say Friday?" And he's like, "No, I've got no email, I've got no internet, I've got nothing." Brandon (01:32) My god. Yes, it's been an interesting week. So Jess, catch us up on everything that's fallen apart in the past few days. We've got quite a list growing here. Jessica Lyons (01:40) Yes. Well, we'll start with Outlook. I'm sorry, Mic

So Jess, catch us up on everything that's fallen apart in the past few days. We've got quite a list growing here. Jessica Lyons (01:40) Yes. Well, we'll start with Outlook. I'm sorry, Microsoft. It was larger than just Outlook, but similar to Liam, I got this message from my dad. We were at dinner with some friends and he said, "What is going on? I haven't been able to access Outlook all day. What is happening?" So this happened last week and there was this massive Microsoft outage and ultimately, people assumed it was maybe a cyber attack. Is somebody DDoSing Microsoft? What's going on? And then a few days later, Microsoft said, "No, this was a faulty software update that we pushed back in July, and it's affecting all of our 365 services now." So that was last Thursday. Then a day later, the FAA grounded all planes . Brandon (02:29) Right. Jessica Lyons (02:29) And again, in light of Microsoft, people were still having problems with Microsoft. All the planes are grounded. At the time, we just knew it was some type of communication error. And that sounds like something that a lot of nation states would really like to hit and attack. And this one, we ultimately learned that it was due to a network upgrade. Their provider, L3Harris, was switching out the copper wiring with fiber. And this has been an ongoing project. Also, kind of seems like maybe Friday the 13th isn't the best day to undertake this. Brandon (03:03) I hadn't even thought about the fact that it was Friday the 13th that all that happened. Jessica Lyons (03:09) So we see that right after Microsoft. And there was kind of a lull over the weekend, which was nice. Chase later said it was a software bug in an on-premises hardware system, and they said it wasn't a cyber attack. Then the next day, the classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for their internal communications went offline. This is really classified stuff that they are communicating about internally. This went offline and when something at a secretive government agency like the NSA goes offline, immediately the first thought is, "Who's attacking us?" The agency later said this was due to scheduled routine maintenance. And actually I almost forgot: Tuesday, Apple had a bunch of issues. It was affecting different services like Apple Support, iCloud, Apple Pay, and their retail stores. There were people waiting in lines because they had some tech issue that they wanted to get help with, and they're not able to get any help because Apple's offline as well. So we have all these outages at these major agencies and companies over the last week. So everybody automatically goes to, "Who's attacking us? Who is responsible for this?" What people assume to be a massive coordinated cyber attack And that wasn't the case. Brandon (04:50) Right. In pretty much every instance. Liam, Canonical was having an outage too, right? Liam Proven (04:53) Yes. I was going to say, we didn't notice the FAA very much in Europe, but Canonical got hit by a distributed denial of service attack. I probably don't need to spell that out. At the end of last week, just before their now semi-annual Ubuntu Summit, which is when they have a bunch of talks about what's coming up and what's new. They've been hit by a number of attacks before. It was very bad timing. Some of their services stayed up. Brandon (05:29) So this was actually attributable to an attack though. Liam Proven (05:32) I believe in this case it looks like it was another DDoS, but it's not the first time. It's not obvious in the open source world that sometimes big, very visible projects are actually from tiny companies. And sometimes things that don't look so important actually have huge companies behind them. But Canonical is not a very big company. And they're a hundred percent remote company. They don't really have headquarters. There's this lovely office which is part of a floor of one building in London, but not that many people work there. It's all hot desks. It's relatively easy to take such a distributed company offline. And so it's becoming hard to say whether some of these things really are due to attacks or due to general vulnerabilities that are being maybe not even exploited, just massive scale attempts to exploit them. And it's not sometimes targeting anybody in particular. There's just a million bots trying to take down PHP and loads of things run on PHP. So you've got PHP in your infrastructure and that means you're not taken down, but your servers are struggling under the load. The number of bots that are trying to crawl all kinds of websites and things constitutes effectively a DDoS at the moment, although it's not really a true DDoS. Brandon (07:16) Right. It's not intentional. It just becomes one by volume. Liam Proven (07:22) So it's actually becoming a little bit moot what exactly constitutes a denial of service attack versus merely being under extremely heavy load. I'm

item.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
item.description: A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels. Read more Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet? The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency. Advertisement But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” , but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates. Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change. Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”. Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance
item.dc:creator: Madeleine Cuff
item.content:encoded: A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels. Read more Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet? The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency. Advertisement But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” , but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates. Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change. Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”. Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries. Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas. Read more The secret weapon that could finally force climate action What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.” Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare , the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement. But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process? The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision. With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful. Read more The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says. The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says. There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week . Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable. UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

item.title: Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad
item.description: US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China. Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose. Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country." The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said. The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X. We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer. Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here." The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week. "We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added. Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it. Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses. Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat. "There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register . "So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences." Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the c
item.dc:creator: Dan Robinson
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China. Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose. Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country." The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said. The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X. We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer. Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here." The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week. "We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added. Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it. Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses. Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat. "There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register . "So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences." Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the cloud giants operate datacenters outside the US, such as latency and regulatory compliance. "A buyer in Frankfurt won't wait for a page to load from Virginia. Some countries require certain data to stay inside their borders, and big European clients write it into contracts anyway," he stated. Trump claimed that communities in America that host datacenters are "making so much money that they don't know what to do with it." Those claimed benefits come alongside substantial public subsidies. Nonprofit organization Good Jobs First reported earlier this year that some states are losing billions in revenue because of the tax abatement schemes offered to companies to entice them to set up shop there. ®

item.title: Esposito emulates Vieri with Inter hat-trick but De Ketelaere haunts him again
item.description: Italy’s new cover star enjoyed a ‘beautiful’ treble but could not celebrate it after his side threw away two-goal leads three times to draw 4-4 with Atalanta This ought to have been a magic moment for Pio Esposito. He had just scored his first Serie A hat-trick, becoming only the third Italian to get one for Inter in the era of three points for a win. The last to do it was Christian Vieri, back in 2003. Two years before Esposito was born. We will come back to that. Esposito has been drawing premature comparisons to Vieri for some time and especially now after a barnstorming November in which he has scored eight times in five games, including three in two for his country, and two of those as part of a man-of-the-match performance during an upset win against France . Continue reading...

item.title: AI conquered chess. What happened next should give us hope
item.description: As two 20-year-old prodigies prepare to battle in the world chess championship, the game offers a surprising lesson about AI and what it cannot replicate The upcoming world chess championship between Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov and India’s Gukesh Dommaraju in Geneva has all the makings of a barnburner. Earlier this year, Sindarov, 20, won the Candidates Tournament as an outside longshot with a magnificent attacking style that overwhelmed the competition, locking up his title shot with a string of dazzling early wins. Continue reading...

item.title: I’m planning my first dark sky trip, and all because this educational star projector showed me what I’m missing
item.description: I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it. Instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution . A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images. Brainstorm Night Sky Projector review Whatever your age, the Brainstorm Night Sky is so simple to use The Brainstorm Night Sky projector comes with four or six slides, depending on whether you buy the blue or gray version (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy. Depending on the model you buy, you’ll get four or six interchangeable slides. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Specifications Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g) Bulb type: Non-specified Laser: No Control: On-unit Rotation: Yes, one speed Projection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m) Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins) Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank. There’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase. This projector revealed what light pollution had taken from me There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. item.dc:creator: Chris McMullen
item.content:encoded: I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it. Instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution . A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images. Brainstorm Night Sky Projector review Whatever your age, the Brainstorm Night Sky is so simple to use The Brainstorm Night Sky projector comes with four or six slides, depending on whether you buy the blue or gray version (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy. Depending on the model you buy, you’ll get four or six interchangeable slides. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Specifications Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g) Bulb type: Non-specified Laser: No Control: On-unit Rotation: Yes, one speed Projection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m) Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins) Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank. There’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase. This projector revealed what light pollution had taken from me There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. Chris McMullen There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. Chris McMullen There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. Chris McMullen The Brainstorm Night Sky model I tested comes with four slides, each with a case to protect them from smudges and sticky fingers. You place one into the provided slide housing then insert that into the projector. There’s the moon, the solar system, and two showing the Northern Hemisphere’s night sky, as seen from Hawaii (a key location for astronomy). I can appreciate the educational value of the first couple, even if I am still seething at Pluto being demoted back in 2006. But it was the latter pair of slides that really opened my eyes to what I could be seeing over my head. I can spot maybe 10-20 stars from my backyard, cloud cover permitting; thanks to light pollution , that’s it. Even though the best stargazing apps can show me what I should see, when I step outside, all I typically see with the naked eye is the odd pinprick in the void. The Brainstorm Night Sky uses three AA batteries, but they’re not included with the projector. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) But as soon as I inserted that third slide, a striking stellar display appeared above my head, with more stars than I could hope to count. Even knowing that Hawaii’s night sky stretches far further than eight feet across, the difference between this view and the one from my house was like night and day. Brainstorm claims this slide features over 20,000 stars, though that’s likely referring to the source photo rather than the projected image. The fourth slide — the same crisp starscape but with every visible constellation labelled — was almost as attention-grabbing. Educational value aside, it drove home that I couldn’t see the majority of these star patterns to name them, my local night sky is that polluted. Knowing what I was missing out on made me determined to take my stargazing further afield. Some of the best smart telescopes can lessen the impact of light pollution, but stepping away from skyglow is the most effective option. Hawaii’s a little far to travel, but I’ve already started looking into local dark sky sites. I just need to grab a pair of the best binoculars for stargazing , hop on my bike and I’m ready to go. The Brainstorm Night Sky is a solid, budget-priced educational tool, but it has one drawback You can purchase one additional Southern Hemisphere slide, but beyond that you’re limited to the included slides. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) The Brainstorm Night Sky’s projections are crisp enough that you can easily make out every constellation name, but they could be a hair brighter. The Ainael Meter Galaxy Projector , for example, delivers more illumination. If you want to use the Brainstorm Night Sky to relax, the rotate function gives its projections an oddly hypnotic effect, and the device is whisper-quiet to boot. And while Brainstorm doesn’t specify battery life, one set of rechargeables lasted me for several days. Unfortunately, the Brainstorm Night Sky's slide collection is a little limited. There are two models, a blue version with four slides (the one I tested) and a gray version with six slides (featuring additional space shuttle and black hole images). The included instructions state you can purchase an additional slide disc showing the Southern Hemisphere’s stars, but that’s a maximum of seven images. Nor is this projector compatible with the slides from the Brainstorm Deep Sky Projector It’s a little disappointing given that Brainstorm has clearly put thought into the projector’s educational value. Those instructions double as a poster of the solar system, and children can use a “secret code” (printed on the instructions) to explore more astronomy facts on the company’s website. Offering extra slide packs, of the kind you can buy for the Pococo Galaxy Projector , would give it more long-term appeal. As is, I can see its novelty and educational value diminishing over time, at which point you can upgrade to one of the best star projectors . If you’re not bothered by the lack of expandability, the Brainstorm Night Sky’s price, image quality and ease of use still make it a useful tool for kindling a child’s interest in astronomy, or as a budget-friendly gift for junior stargazers. It’s certainly spurred me into action — how much is a plane ticket to Hawaii, anyway?

item.title: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?
item.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been. So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure? Last of the Soviet space explorers Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June. A model of one of the Phobos spacecraft on display in the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics in Moscow, Russia. (Image credit: Музей Космонавтики from Россия, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons) To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989 , when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues. Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team. item.dc:creator: Micah Hanks
item.content:encoded:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been. So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure? Last of the Soviet space explorers Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June. A model of one of the Phobos spacecraft on display in the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics in Moscow, Russia. (Image credit: Музей Космонавтики from Россия, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons) To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989 , when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues. Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team. An image of Phobos captured by the Soviet Union's Phobos 2 probe. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Unexplained failure That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April. Achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe. An image of Mars and its moon Phobos captured by the Soviet Union's Phobos 2 spacecraft on Feb. 28, 1989. Phobos 2 took a total of 13 color sets of images of Phobos before contact was lost on March 27, 1989. (Image credit: Roscosmos) A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power. No further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown. Theories involving the failure Although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland , one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out. The final image transmitted from the Soviet Union's Phobos 2 spacecraft shortly before losing communication with Earth. (Image credit: Roscosmos) A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical issues as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss. However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise. The shadow in Phobos 2's final photos Soviet test pilot Marina Popovich. (Image credit: Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images) In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft. Among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership . Given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate. Explaining the Phobos "shadow" Determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note , due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature." In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time. item.title: New Outlook's attachment issues sent users into the arms of its predecessor
item.description: A recent update broke attachment handling for some New Outlook users, prompting Microsoft to recommend switching to the web or Classic version of its email client. Things are going swimmingly for New Outlook, the email client that Microsoft would very much like users to migrate to. A code change meant that for some users, opening or uploading email attachments failed. It took the company two attempts to fix the problem. Microsoft confirmed there were issues on November 20, as reports that customers were having problems with attachments began rolling in. By the end of the day, the company had added inline images in email to the litany of woe and "paused the rollout of a recent client update that may be contributing to attachment failures." The advice for affected users was to switch to the web version, or use Outlook Classic to open or upload attachments and view inline images. The good news was that Microsoft produced a fix. The bad news was that this fix only resolved problems with Office attachments and inline images, leaving other attachment types affected, according to incident notice EX1561765. The Windows behemoth tried again with a "supplemental fix" and reported the remaining problems resolved on November 21. Users needed to close and reopen New Outlook for the fix to take effect. Microsoft said it had tested the fixes before deployment. Administrators might reasonably wish the original update had received the same attention. The preliminary root cause was a "recent update to the code which supports embedded web content unexpectedly caused impact." The clock is ticking for Outlook Classic. Microsoft is clear that New Outlook is the future, though Classic Outlook will remain available until at least 2029. The fact that the company had to suggest that affected users fall back on the old warhorse to perform that rarely used email activity – attachment handling – is less than confidence-inspiring. Still, by the time Outlook Classic is finally put out to pasture, we're sure Microsoft's habit of sending out broken updates will also be a thing of the past. Right? ®

item.title: Norway links energy firm cyberattacks to critical Azure API Management flaw
item.description: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations. According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register , Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies , only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2. It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault. Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration. The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs. Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote . "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets. The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise. NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations. The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation. "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said . "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. "When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses." Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear. Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied. NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched. Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

item.title: Jamal Musiala controversy the nadir of Bayern Munich’s turbulent week
item.description: German giants’ treatment of midfielder has raised questions about how far the reputation of a family club still holds It was, on paper, a perfect Friday evening for Bayern to flex their muscles once again, in the chill of their intimidating Allianz Arena against struggling opponents who had won just twice all season in the league. In the end, though, the best news of the night was that Saïd El Mala, the star of the visitors, Köln, who had scored a jaw-dropping consolation goal at the same stadium in spring, fluffed a far easier chance in the closing stages that would have condemned the champions to defeat. The word crisis is rampantly overused in sport, but this was the weekend Bayern’s injury troubles reached critical mass. With Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry and Ismaël Saibari already missing, their talisman Harry Kane had his game curtailed after 20 minutes and by the time the second half had begun, they’d lost Michael Olise too. item.title: Cleverbridge admits attackers stole customers' credit card and CVV numbers. Yep, you read that right
item.description: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization. The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update , Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems. The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register , fills in some rather important blanks. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers. Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach. More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach. Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk. That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems. In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion. Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase. Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®

item.title: Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show
item.description: Management team were in line for huge payouts Fifa denies Infantino would have profited from plan Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian. Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. They outline a plan, produced days before July’s final of the 2026 World Cup, to profit from the sport’s burgeoning commercial revenues for almost a century. Continue reading...

item.title: Capita CEO leaves following pensions contract disaster
item.description: Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect as the outsourcer warned of sharply lower profits next year, nearly a year after its troubled takeover of administration of the UK's Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS). In a statement , Capita said CFO Pablo Andres had become CEO, with group financial controller Gemma Bate-Williams succeeding him as finance chief. Capita now expects adjusted operating profit for 2027 to be £85 million to £95 million below previous expectations. That includes £15 million to £25 million in additional costs under a pensions recovery plan agreed with the Cabinet Office, alongside pressure from contract exits and other trading headwinds. Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement. The company – which is also coming under fire for its £370 million contract with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) – said it had made significant progress in its transformation and strategic simplification. It also plans to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 to reduce borrowing and to "allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation," subject to support from its financial creditors. James Preece, principal analyst at UK tech research firm Megabuyte, said: "Slow motion car crash comes to mind. It has been a turnaround job for coming up to four years now, with long-suffering shareholders watching dozens of disposals and business exits fail to arrest a structural decline in both margins and growth. "Today's update suggests that management's underlying forecast assumptions alongside other more transient factors were still too punchy, and the leverage situation now calls for action. The share price reaction suggests confidence in this being a one-and-done raise is limited," he said. Capita took over administration of the scheme in December 2025 under a seven-year, £239 million contract, after which The Register exclusively revealed problems with its online systems . The vendor promised AI and automation, but the takeover brought a glitchy online portal, while some members struggled to receive pension payments. By January, it was clear the service was seriously failing, leaving some retired civil servants struggling to make ends meet. Capita missed its deadline to restore normal service by the end of June. It subsequently told MPs that all but the most complex cases would return to normal service by September. The pensions scheme serves around 1.7 million members. Media reports and MPs have described members feeling upset, frustrated, and ignored, with some waiting months for payments. The government said it had withheld £10 million in payments over Capita's performance during the transition of the pensions service and was negotiating further penalties. It also appointed an auditor to assess the case for further penalties for Capita's performance on the contract. Last month, the National Audit Office launched an investigation into the CSPS contract. Res
item.dc:creator: Lindsay Clark
item.content:encoded: Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect as the outsourcer warned of sharply lower profits next year, nearly a year after its troubled takeover of administration of the UK's Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS). In a statement , Capita said CFO Pablo Andres had become CEO, with group financial controller Gemma Bate-Williams succeeding him as finance chief. Capita now expects adjusted operating profit for 2027 to be £85 million to £95 million below previous expectations. That includes £15 million to £25 million in additional costs under a pensions recovery plan agreed with the Cabinet Office, alongside pressure from contract exits and other trading headwinds. Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement. The company – which is also coming under fire for its £370 million contract with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) – said it had made significant progress in its transformation and strategic simplification. It also plans to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 to reduce borrowing and to "allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation," subject to support from its financial creditors. James Preece, principal analyst at UK tech research firm Megabuyte, said: "Slow motion car crash comes to mind. It has been a turnaround job for coming up to four years now, with long-suffering shareholders watching dozens of disposals and business exits fail to arrest a structural decline in both margins and growth. "Today's update suggests that management's underlying forecast assumptions alongside other more transient factors were still too punchy, and the leverage situation now calls for action. The share price reaction suggests confidence in this being a one-and-done raise is limited," he said. Capita took over administration of the scheme in December 2025 under a seven-year, £239 million contract, after which The Register exclusively revealed problems with its online systems . The vendor promised AI and automation, but the takeover brought a glitchy online portal, while some members struggled to receive pension payments. By January, it was clear the service was seriously failing, leaving some retired civil servants struggling to make ends meet. Capita missed its deadline to restore normal service by the end of June. It subsequently told MPs that all but the most complex cases would return to normal service by September. The pensions scheme serves around 1.7 million members. Media reports and MPs have described members feeling upset, frustrated, and ignored, with some waiting months for payments. The government said it had withheld £10 million in payments over Capita's performance during the transition of the pensions service and was negotiating further penalties. It also appointed an auditor to assess the case for further penalties for Capita's performance on the contract. Last month, the National Audit Office launched an investigation into the CSPS contract. Responding to the investigation, Capita said it "accepts that performance remains below the standards that scheme members and the Government rightly expect" and that fixing the problems was its top priority. The Public and Commercial Services Union is campaigning to get the government to scrap a separate Capita contract, the Synergy shared services deal, which Capita values at £370 million. The deal covers HR, payroll, finance, and other back-office services across four government departments and nearly 100 arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, has also launched a legal challenge alleging Capita's bid was abnormally low. Capita and the DWP – which leads on the contract – have denied the allegations. ®

item.title: Astronomers just discovered a rare triple star system 28 light-years away, and they have ‘no clean explanation for how it got here’
item.description: A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system. "We were actually looking for planets ," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement . "Instead, we found something much more surprising." So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years . Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here." This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects. A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity . This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across. Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass . Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as quickly. One of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located much farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair, revealing the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) detected using the Gemini North telescope's 'Alopeke instrument. item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system. "We were actually looking for planets ," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement . "Instead, we found something much more surprising." So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years . Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here." This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects. A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity . This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across. Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass . Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as quickly. One of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual. Observations of the Welopō'ai triple-star system, located 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located much farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair, revealing the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) detected using the Gemini North telescope's 'Alopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the stars' orbital paths. (Image credit: Photo : Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST (left); International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab (right). Graphic compilation: Étienne Artigau and Heidi White (UdeM/IREx)) SPIRou discovers planets by measuring how much their gravity tugs on their host star. Think of a star and planet orbiting a kind of gravitational balancing point between them called a center of mass. This center of mass is usually inside the star, since the star is far more massive than the planet, but crucially not at its very center, so the star appears to wobble to and fro around the combined center of mass. The spectrometer measures this wobble in the form of a Doppler shift in the star's light that can be translated into the velocity at which the star is moving around this center of mass. Astronomers call this a 'radial velocity'. A large gas giant like Jupiter might incur a radial velocity of hundreds of meters per second, while an Earth-mass planet generates a radial velocity of tens of meters. Yet the object that SPIRou found orbiting close to the red dwarf was creating a huge radial velocity signals of 10 miles (16 kilometers) per second. Whatever it was, it was not a planet. With the help of the eight-meter Gemini North telescope on Hawaii's Mauna Kea, Artigau's team were able to identify the mystery object as a white dwarf. "The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star," said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and a co-author of the study. White dwarfs are not exactly rare, and even finding two white dwarfs together is not unheard of: WD 0727+482 is a binary white dwarf system 37 light-years away, for example. To encounter two white dwarfs in a triple system with a regular star though is a precious find. The reason being that the masses of white dwarfs are not generally well defined. Yet their masses are not random; they are directly connected to the mass of the star that produced them. Thanks to the newly discovered white dwarf being separated from the red dwarf by about 4.6 astronomical units (688 million kilometers/428 million miles) – that's closer than Jupiter orbits our sun – Artigau's team were able to measure their masses to within an uncertainty of less than 1%. They found that the red dwarf has a mass 42% that of our sun and the newly discovered white dwarf has a mass 62% that of our sun. When the white dwarf was a regular star it would have had a mass 40% greater than our sun. The second more distant white dwarf orbits the pair of them. The Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, which helped identify the stars in the Welopō'ai triple system. (Image credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/J. Warner) The Welopō'ai system is therefore a good system for testing our models of stellar evolution that dictate how massive a white dwarf should be. If we know the white dwarf's mass with high precision, scientists can also use that as a starting point from which to explore the extreme physics of the white dwarf's condensed matter, which is being held up and prevented from contracting any further by something called electron degeneracy pressure – the unwillingness of negatively charged electrons to crush down any further and merge with positively charged protons to form neutrons . That takes the extra gravity from a more massive star to form a neutron star . So why should Welopō'ai not exist? The trouble is that when stars turn into red giants they really stir things up. Even if the red giant didn't expand out as far as the red dwarf, the expansion should have destabilized the red dwarf's orbit and potentially even caused it to crash into the red giant. Yet here the red dwarf is in a happily stable orbit like nothing had happened. "That is the question driving our next observations," said Dufour. It is hoped that further, more detailed, measurements of the gravitational interactions between the three members of the Welopō'ai system will help the team disentangle the evolutionary history of the trio to better understand their orbits and how the red dwarf survived. And because they are so relatively close to us, we have the advantage of being able to make high-precision measurements. "Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises," said Artigau. "Even when we're searching for planets, our universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us." The discovery of the Welopō'ai triple system is described in a paper published on Nov. 19 in Astronomy & Astrophysics .

item.title: From Mind Games to Ghost Stories! 5 Nollywood Titles to Stream This Week
item.description: Wande Thomas’s psychological thriller Spiraling, starring Toni Tones, Jim Iyke, Folu Storms and Seun Ajayi on KAVA, is among the titles recommended to watch this week. Wrongfully accused, caught in a web of lies, pulled into a dangerous family feud or haunted by a past you never saw coming. This week’s streaming picks have a little bit of everything for anyone who enjoys a story that refuses to let them relax. We’ve rounded up five titles across Circuits, Netflix, Prime Video and KAVA, taking you from psychological thrillers and gang conflicts to supernatural mysteries and a night out that spirals into something much bigger. Extra Mile — Circuits Sometimes trying to do a good deed for someone else is how everything goes sideways. That is the trap at the heart of this drama, where a woman ends up behind bars for a crime she never committed after stepping in to help a friend. Mercy Johnson – Okojie , Jim Iyke and Lilian Esoro carry the story forward under Kayode Kasum ‘s direction, working from a screenplay by Folasade Osibo and with Joy Grant – Ekong and Solate Ovundah – Akarolo on board as producers. Double Decoy — Circuits Moving from courtroom-style heartbreak straight into psychological mind games, our next pick on the same platform turns suspicion into a sport. Nothing looks straightforward when hidden agendas, shifting loyalties and high-stakes deception collide in this tense thriller. As every move feels like a test of trust, viewers are left guessing who is really pulling the strings, anchored by Kanayo O . Kanayo , Sola Sobowale and Gideon Okeke . Behind the scenes, the credits point to Oluwafemi Isaac Akinsipe alongside Nnamdi E . Odunze and Chichi Stylxz . The Covenant Season 2 — Netflix If that kind of high-stakes tension gets you in the mood for bigger battles and family rivalries, head over to Netflix next where the stakes climb even higher. Picking up right where the first run left off, the second season plunges deeper into power struggles, family loyalty and survival as Dagogo gets pulled further into dangerous conflicts and old scores. Gideon Okeke is back alongside Uzee Usman in a story created by Vincent Okonkwo and directed by Menelik Shabazz (“menelikfather”), mixing tense action, supernatural undertones and shifting alliances that keep the pressure on. Ajuwaya 2: Ghost of Selema — Prime Video Trading gang wars and big empires for eerie small-town secrets, our next stop on Prime Video shifts the tension somewhere much closer to home. Imagine posting up for youth service in a new town only to become the fixation of a troubled young man—and then digging into his past and finding a secret that links him straight to you with every reason to haunt you. Tolu LordTanner directs this suspenseful drama starring Godspower Nwogwugwu , Damilola Onitilo , Oyeyemi Adeoye and Ovy Godwin . Spiraling — KAVA From a haunting in a service town, we finish the week with a glossy, high-tension spiral set between Lagos and Abuja. What starts as a nig
